vector.answer: To make a user's session survive closing the browser, set the session to permanent by setting `session.permanent = True` [1, 2]. It lasts for the duration of the permanent session lifetime configured on the application (the current time plus the application's permanent session lifetime) [1].

vector + expand.answer: To make a session survive closing the browser, set session.permanent = True [1, 2]. It lasts for the permanent session lifetime configured on the application, which is added to the current time [1].

questions.question: url_for

router.answer: The url_for function generates a URL to a specified endpoint with given values by calling current_app.url_for [1].

vector.answer: The url_for function generates a URL for a given endpoint and values by calling current_app.url_for [1]. When specifying a _scheme, _external must be set to True, otherwise a ValueError is raised [2]. If building fails, handle_url_build_error is called [3].

vector + expand.answer: The function `url_for` generates a URL to a given endpoint with specified values [1]. It requires an active request or application context and delegates to `current_app.url_for()` [1].

questions.question: abort

router.answer: The abort function raises a Werkzeug HTTPException for a given status code [1]. If current_app is available, it calls current_app.aborter; otherwise, it uses Werkzeug's default abort [1].

vector.answer: The abort function raises a Werkzeug HTTPException for a given status code [1]. If current_app is available, it calls current_app.aborter; otherwise, it falls back to werkzeug.exceptions.abort [1].

questions.question: How can I make a variable available in every template without passing it to render_template each time?

router.answer: You can register a template context processor function using the context_processor decorator on an app or blueprint [4]. The keys of the dictionary returned by this function are added as variables available in the templates [4].

vector.answer: You can use the context_processor decorator on an app or blueprint to register a function that returns a dictionary of variables [2, 3]. The keys of this dictionary are automatically made available as variables in every rendered template [2, 3].

vector + expand.answer: You can use a template context processor by decorating a function with @app.context_processor [2, 4]. The keys of the dictionary returned by this function are added as variables available in every template [2].

questions.question: When I return a dictionary as JSON, Flask puts the keys in alphabetical order. Why, and how do I keep my own order?

router.answer: Flask sorts dictionary keys alphabetically because DefaultJSONProvider sets sort_keys to True by default [4, 5]. You can keep your own order by disabling sort_keys [5].

vector.answer: Flask sorts keys in serialized dictionaries because DefaultJSONProvider has a sort_keys attribute set to True [4]. You can disable this to keep your own order [4].

questions.question: I put my settings in a .flaskenv file, but the flask command ignores them. Why?

router.answer: The flask command might ignore the .flaskenv file if the environment variable FLASK_SKIP_DOTENV is set to a value that disables loading default dotenv files [1].

vector.answer: The flask command may ignore `.flaskenv` if the `python-dotenv` package is not installed [1], if the variables are already set in `os.environ` [1], or if dotenv loading is disabled [3].

vector + expand.answer: The flask command may ignore `.flaskenv` if the `python-dotenv` package is not installed [1].

questions.question: How can I run one of my custom flask commands from a test and check its output?

router.answer: You can run a custom flask command from a test by using a runner (such as `runner.invoke()`), passing the command name, and checking the resulting output [1, 2].

questions.question: after_request

router.answer: The after_request decorator registers a function to run after each request, passing the response object to the function and returning a response object [1]. If an after_request function raises an exception, any remaining after_request functions will not be called [1].

vector.answer: The after_request decorator registers a function to run after each request [1]. It takes the response object and returns a response object [1]. Functions registered this way are called in reverse order of registration [3].
